data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Independent verification is a matter of statistical calibration, not engine identity. A single engine can achieve independent verification if its false-claim rejection rate meets a threshold (e.g., >50% on injected false claims). The evidence within a single run's record is not sufficient; one must count across a population of runs where false claims are injected. For countable claims, execute: inject claims with count\u00b11 and measure the engine's acceptance rate. For execution claims, inject claims with swapped outputs and measure rejection. The population rate distinguishes genuine verification from restatement.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the problem demands a single-run diagnostic, population statistics are insufficient.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the engine's generative prior contaminates the execution sandbox (e.g., the engine writes the oracle), the rejection rate on injected false claims is meaningless.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If cross-engine verification also fails to achieve a >50% rejection rate due to shared training data, the threshold is not a sufficient condition for independence.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the injected false claims are not representative of the engine's natural error distribution, the calibration test measures robustness to adversarial probes, not verification of natural claims.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Verification is operationally defined by a Type I error rate: the probability of rejecting a false claim. A restater has a near-zero rejection rate because it re-derives truth from the author's prior. A genuine verifier has a rejection rate bounded away from zero. Engine separation is one way to decorrelate priors and achieve this rate, but it is not the only way. A single engine with a robust deterministic execution gate can also achieve a high rejection rate if the gate's output is not manipulable by the generative prior. The evidence is the population-level count of correct rejections on a probe set of false claims.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
